vignette:
He is 23, a young urban planner who once moved through the city with a kind of hopeful precision. Before the assault, he spends his days studying traffic flow, pedestrian safety, and public space, tracing on maps how people live together. He likes order, clear routes, and the feeling that a place can be made safer if someone pays enough attention. He is quiet, thoughtful, and usually keeps to himself. Being single suits him, he says; work gives structure to his week, and the city itself feels like something he understands.

The assault happens late one evening after he leaves the office. He has stayed behind to finish a proposal and misses the bus he usually takes. He decides to walk part of the way home through a commercial area he knows well, a route he has taken many times without thinking. At first nothing feels unusual. Then he notices footsteps behind him, quick and uneven, before a man comes up beside him and demands his phone and wallet. He freezes for a second, confused by how fast the moment changes. When he hesitates, the man hits him hard across the face and shoves him to the ground. He remembers the concrete against his hands, the taste of blood in his mouth, and the sound of his own breathing becoming ragged and loud. The attacker kicks him in the ribs, grabs his bag, and runs. What stays with him most is not only the pain but the helplessness—how suddenly his body stops belonging to him, how the street he knows becomes unrecognizable.

In the first days after, he tells himself he is lucky to be alive. He returns to work quickly, downplays the bruising, and gives a short version of the story when colleagues ask. But the city has changed for him. Walking to the office, he scans every face, every doorway, every figure lingering near a bus stop. If he hears footsteps behind him, his chest tightens before he can think. He starts taking expensive rides instead of walking, then feels ashamed at how much money he is spending just to avoid being outside. At work, he finds himself staring at maps of neighborhoods and thinking not about zoning or transport corridors but about where someone could be cornered, where sightlines are poor, where escape would be difficult. He notices blind spots everywhere.

Sleep becomes the place where the assault keeps happening. He wakes suddenly, soaked in sweat, heart pounding, convinced for a moment that someone is standing over him. Some nights he dreams the attacker has no face. Other nights, the man’s face keeps changing into strangers he sees during the day. He begins sleeping with the lights on, then with a chair pushed against the door, embarrassed by how childish it feels and unable to stop. By morning he is exhausted and irritable. He misses deadlines he would once have met easily. During meetings, if someone speaks too loudly or comes up behind his chair, he jolts so sharply that others pause and look at him. He laughs it off, but inside he feels exposed.

He tries to regain control by narrowing his life. He no longer goes out after dark. He avoids the street where the assault happened, then the whole district around it. He stops meeting friends for dinner because the thought of returning home at night fills him with dread. When his mother calls from abroad and asks how he is doing, he says work is busy. He cannot bear her worry, and he cannot find words for the fear that now follows him into ordinary places. Being alone, which once felt peaceful, now becomes a trap in which his thoughts circle without relief.

What unsettles him most is how his mind keeps dragging him back. A man reaching into his jacket pocket on the train can make his body tense as if impact is seconds away. The smell of stale beer on a passerby, the slap of running shoes on pavement, even seeing a phone dropped onto concrete can split open the present. In those moments he is no longer on a morning commute or reviewing site plans; he is back on the ground, bracing for another kick. He knows, rationally, that the danger is over, but his body does not believe him.

Now, months later, he speaks about the assault in a flat, controlled voice that occasionally breaks without warning. He says he feels as though the city has expelled him from the version of himself he used to be. The work that once felt meaningful now feels cruelly ironic: he spends his days designing safer public environments while moving through his own life as if nowhere is safe. He wants the old ease of walking, the simple anonymity of being one person among many on a city street. Instead he lives in a state of watchfulness, tired and ashamed of being afraid, longing for an ordinary evening that does not feel like a test of survival.
